title: The China Squeeze: A response to our critics
gist: Rebutting Adam Tooze and other critics, Chatterjee and Subramanian argue that China's persistent dominance of low-skill manufacturing exports is quantitatively anomalous (its global export share has risen since 1995 even as its share of the world's unskilled labor force fell) and is actively foreclosing industrialization in low- and middle-income countries. Their hard evidence is the surge in LMIC anti-dumping measures against China (from ~13 per year in 2000-2014 to 33 in 2021-2025, hitting 52 by 2025) and the co-movement of China's export share with the renminbi since the mid-2010s, which they read as proof that policy distortions, not just supply-chain efficiency, are at work.

themes.theme: Squeeze is global, not an India story

insights.claim: The 'China Squeeze' thesis - that Chinese manufacturing export strength forecloses poorer countries' path to industrialization - is framed around low- and middle-income countries generally, not India specifically, despite critics reading it as an Indian preoccupation.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Positions the squeeze as a systemic emerging-market growth constraint, not a bilateral India-China narrative - relevant to any EM industrialization or frontier-market growth thesis.
insights.locator: 1. An Indian concern

insights.claim: ASEAN policymakers have long debated how to handle what the authors call the Chinese export juggernaut, indicating the competitive pressure is a live policy issue across Southeast Asia rather than a Western or Indian talking point.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Expect continued ASEAN trade-defense and localization policy risk for firms routing Chinese goods through the region.

insights.claim: Around 60 textile factories in Indonesia closed between 2022 and 2025, and student riots there have been attributed to shrinking industrialization caused by Chinese competition.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Import competition in light manufacturing is now a social-stability and political-risk variable in Indonesia - watch for abrupt protectionist measures against Chinese textiles.
insights.locator: Student riots in Indonesia have been attributed

insights.claim: Deindustrialization pressure from Chinese competition has escalated into street-level political unrest in at least one large emerging market, linking trade flows directly to domestic instability.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Treat EM manufacturing-employment erosion as a leading indicator of political risk premia, not just a trade-balance line item.
insights.locator: Student riots in Indonesia have been attributed

insights.claim: Anti-dumping measures imposed by low- and middle-income countries against Chinese companies have risen from negligible levels to 52 by 2025.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: A hard, trackable series for gauging when EM trade barriers against Chinese goods will bite - a rising count signals tariff and quota risk for China-exposed exporters.
insights.locator: It is not just in the reporting

insights.claim: The average number of LMIC anti-dumping measures against China rose from about 13 per year over 2000-2014 to 33 per year over 2021-2025, while anti-dumping investigations roughly tripled from about 15 to 54 across the same periods.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Investigations (54) run ahead of measures (33-52), so the pipeline implies further EM trade restrictions on Chinese goods over the next several years.
insights.locator: The average number of measures increased

insights.claim: India has imposed the most anti-dumping measures against China, but Brazil, Turkey, Vietnam, South Africa, Indonesia, Pakistan, Peru, Argentina, Malaysia, and Thailand have all been consistent users.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: A named watchlist of EMs most likely to escalate trade defense against China - relevant for supply-chain routing and local-champion equity plays in those markets.
insights.locator: India has the highest number of such measures

insights.claim: Legal trade-defense actions filed by developing countries are the most credible evidence of their concern about Chinese competition, because they are costly revealed preference rather than rhetoric.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Use anti-dumping filing counts, not official statements, as the real-time gauge of EM tolerance for Chinese import penetration.
insights.locator: In some ways, these actions are the real reflection

insights.claim: The rise in anti-dumping measures against China broadly tracks the rise in China's global export market share, which peaked in the mid-2010s.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Trade-barrier intensity is a lagged function of export-share gains, so any renewed China export-share surge should be underwritten with a rising protectionism cost.
insights.locator: This rise broadly corresponds to the rise

insights.claim: The reason Chinese competitive pressure looks absent in third markets is not that it is absent, but that developing countries have no policy instruments to respond there, unlike in their own domestic markets where anti-dumping actions make the pressure visible.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Measurement bias means the true displacement of EM exporters by China is systematically understated - look at lost export share in third markets, not just domestic import surges.
insights.quote: The difference is that in their own markets, they can take action, which is visible; in third markets, they have no instruments to respond.
insights.locator: If competition from China in their own markets

insights.claim: Critics who accept 'China Shock 1.0 and 2.0' as real while dismissing the China Squeeze as merely counterfactual are being inconsistent, since all three scenarios are counterfactual 'what would happen if' constructs.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Analysts who accept China-shock effects on Western manufacturing but discount them for EMs are applying an asymmetric standard - a bias worth correcting in EM industrialization models.
insights.locator: 2. China can Shock the West but not the Rest

insights.claim: It is incoherent to hold that Chinese export capability can damage Western manufacturing but not that of poorer countries, effectively making even victimhood a privilege reserved for rich economies.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Frames a coming shift in the global trade-politics narrative from West-vs-China toward Global-South-vs-China, changing where trade barriers appear next.
insights.quote: Chinese competition is only a reality for the rich West but not the poor Rest, as if even the "privilege" of victimhood is the preserve of the former.
insights.locator: More fundamentally, the distinction suggests

insights.claim: Academic work by Atkin, Costinot, and Fukui, published in the Review of Economic Studies in May 2026, finds that the rise of China has stalled the development of African economies by holding back their growth capability.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Independent peer-reviewed support that Africa's growth ceiling is partly externally imposed - tempers optimism on African manufacturing-led catch-up stories.
insights.locator: Complementing our mechanism is that of Atkin

themes.theme: Domestic failure vs external squeeze: rejecting the binary

insights.claim: Weak domestic capability in developing countries and Chinese competitive pressure are jointly true causes of failed industrialization, not competing explanations - holding domestic capability constant, LMICs would export more if China were less competitive or its policies less assertive.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: EM industrialization forecasts that only model domestic reform (human capital, institutions, policy) will overstate the payoff from those reforms while China's export position holds.
insights.quote: Two things can be true at the same time.
insights.locator: 3. Domestic failures not China Squeeze

insights.claim: Open rich-country markets and China's WTO accession were critical to China's economic success, a point acknowledged even by Chinese scholars and policymakers, contradicting the view that China's rise was purely self-generated.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: If external market access was a necessary condition for China's takeoff, its absence today is a first-order reason to discount catch-up scenarios for the next generation of exporters.
insights.locator: Furthermore, even Chinese scholars and policymakers

insights.claim: Economic convergence generally, and the growth takeoffs of both China and India specifically, coincided with the era of hyperglobalization rather than occurring independently of it.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: In a deglobalizing world the historical base rate for EM convergence is not the right prior - discount long-run growth assumptions for frontier markets accordingly.
insights.locator: That economic convergence in general

themes.theme: Benchmarking the anomaly in China's export share

insights.claim: Around 1995 China's share of global exports was similar to its share of the world's low-skilled labor force, but since then China has lost labor-force share while continuing to gain export market share, opening a quantitatively very large gap.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: The core anomaly metric: the widening wedge between China's export share and its unskilled-labor endowment is what any normalization trade would have to close.
insights.locator: The real puzzle is the evolution of the export market share

insights.claim: The genuine analytical puzzle is not that China exports cars but that a country at its income level is still exporting t-shirts, a framing shared by Yasheng Huang using a different benchmark - the ratio of exports to imports of unskilled goods over time.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Watch China's low-skill export-to-import ratio: Ricardian theory says it should fall with rising wages, and any turn would signal genuine space opening for EM exporters.
insights.quote: The puzzle is not why China exports cars but why it is still exporting t-shirts.
insights.locator: 4. China's dominance not unusual

insights.claim: The argument that China's trade pattern is anomalous is strengthened not by any single benchmark but by the fact that multiple independent benchmarks with different assumptions all point to a departure large enough to warrant the 'unusual' label.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Robustness across methods, not any one statistic, is the reason to treat China's low-skill export dominance as a durable structural constraint rather than a measurement artifact.
insights.locator: What makes the argument serious, even compelling

insights.claim: Ricardian theory predicts a country's ratio of exports to imports of unskilled-labor goods should decline as it develops and wages rise, but China's has risen over time - the opposite of the textbook path.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Standard trade-theory-based assumptions that China will vacate low-end manufacturing as it gets richer have been wrong for three decades and should not anchor EM investment cases.
insights.locator: This is also consistent with Huang's central argument

themes.theme: Efficiency vs distortion: the renminbi test

insights.claim: China's unusual trade performance likely reflects a combination of genuine productivity gains from technology, scale, logistics, supply chains, and organization, and policy-induced distortions including wage suppression and an undervalued exchange rate documented by the IMF and Brad Setser.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: The policy-distortion component is the part that could reverse via currency or wage policy - the efficiency component will not, so separating them sizes any mean-reversion trade.
insights.locator: China's unusual trade performance over time may reflect

insights.claim: The claim that supply-chain network effects are 'overwhelmingly dominant' over policy distortions in explaining China's low-skill export dominance is bold and unsupported by evidence, since no one has established the relative contributions of these factors.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: The efficiency-only explanation is an untested assertion, so do not assume China's export position is immune to policy reversal.
insights.quote: Their effects cannot be dismissed merely by relabeling dominance as efficiency.
insights.locator: Tooze embraces a specific subset

insights.claim: Supply-chain network effects explain why China's advantage persists but do not establish the absence of adverse effects on latecomers - the network effects may themselves be the mechanism through which the squeeze operates.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Agglomeration is not an exculpatory explanation but a barrier-to-entry: it makes the incumbency of Chinese manufacturing harder to dislodge by any friendshoring policy.
insights.locator: First, while Tooze's emphasis on supply chains

insights.claim: Control over supply chains, logistics, and intermediate inputs can itself be distortionary by conferring market power, in the same way that dense incumbency underpins many US antitrust cases against large technology companies.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Imports an antitrust lens into trade policy - a template that could justify structural, not just tariff-based, remedies against Chinese supply-chain dominance.
insights.quote: an incumbent's dense supplier ecosystem can simultaneously raise global efficiency today and make it harder for potential competitors to acquire the capabilities needed tomorrow
insights.locator: Second, control over supply chains

insights.claim: Mattoo, Mishra, and Subramanian (2017) document that renminbi appreciation has a significant positive effect on developing-country exports to third markets, which is precisely the mechanism underlying the China Squeeze.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: A tradable linkage: sustained RMB appreciation should mechanically lift EM export volumes and manufacturing equities in competing exporters.
insights.locator: Mattoo, Mishra, and Subramanian (2017)

insights.claim: China's export share has fallen and risen since the mid-2010s roughly in line with movements in the renminbi, and variation over such short horizons cannot plausibly be explained by slow-moving factors like wage compression or superior efficiency.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Makes the RMB the highest-frequency tradable proxy for the squeeze: watch the currency to time relative performance of competing EM exporters.
insights.locator: Moreover, China's export share has fallen and risen

insights.claim: If the renminbi is undervalued and China's external surplus is large and concentrated enough in low-skill manufacturing to threaten German manufacturing, as Brad Setser argues, then the same forces must be damaging the export performance of competing developing countries.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: A consistency trap for analysts long the German-industrial-pain thesis: the same logic implies a much larger, unpriced drag on EM exporters.

themes.theme: Normative framing and the limits of China-boosterism

insights.claim: The authors concede that today's rich economies never ceded low-skill export space out of benevolence and that China is under no obligation to do so, but argue that where export-space occupation results from Chinese policy intervention, normative conclusions are warranted.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Narrows the policy attack surface to demonstrable distortions (currency, wage suppression), which is where any future multilateral pressure on China will concentrate.
insights.locator: 5. Obligation to "cede" export space

insights.claim: Chinese mercantilism has delivered substantial global benefits including the Great Moderation and the greening of the world economy, even as it imposes costs on developing-country industrialization.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Any unwinding of Chinese export dominance would also unwind disinflation and cheap clean-energy hardware - a two-sided macro risk for rates and energy-transition costs.
insights.locator: A final thought. It is undeniable

insights.claim: Discourse about China has polarized into unseemly China-bashing on one side and China-boosterism or apologism on the other, crowding out serious analysis of the harms of Chinese mercantilism.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Signals that mainstream economic analysis of China's trade harms to the Global South is underdeveloped - an information edge for investors willing to model it.
insights.quote: However, the reflex reaction to that must not be China-boosterism or China-apologism.
insights.locator: A final thought. It is undeniable

insights.claim: If British mercantilism is judged to have caused deindustrialization in the colonies, analytical balance requires subjecting Chinese mercantilism to the same historical scrutiny.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: Frames the squeeze in colonial-era terms - rhetoric that could gain traction in Global South politics and accelerate trade-defense coalitions against China.
insights.quote: China cannot be exempt from historical analysis or indeed placed outside of and beyond history just because we find some current Western attitudes to China disagreeable.
insights.locator: But there should be scope for discussing

insights.claim: The China Squeeze research has drawn a formal response from the Chinese Foreign Ministry, indicating the argument is being treated as consequential at the state level rather than as an academic curiosity.
insights.speaker: Shoumitro Chatterjee,Arvind Subramanian
insights.so_what: State-level pushback suggests Beijing sees reputational risk in the Global South squeeze narrative - watch for conciliatory Chinese trade or investment gestures toward LMICs.
insights.locator: Our work has attracted considerable responses
